ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Bronchial asthma: 4

A patient whose asthma is usually controlled develops wheezing after a viral upper-respiratory illness. There is no focal consolidation or other evidence establishing bacterial pneumonia. Which mechanism best explains this familiar pattern of symptom worsening?

  1. Trigger-associated worsening of airway narrowing
  2. Variable expiratory airflow limitation
  3. Repeat objective testing when symptomatic or use an appropriate variability test
  4. Type 2 airway inflammation
  5. Bronchial hyperresponsiveness
Answer and explanation

Trigger-associated worsening of airway narrowing

Viral infections, allergens and irritants can provoke symptoms in susceptible airways without each episode implying bacterial pneumonia.

Option explanations

Trigger-associated worsening of airway narrowing: Viral infections, allergens and irritants can provoke symptoms in susceptible airways without each episode implying bacterial pneumonia.

Variable expiratory airflow limitation: Episodic symptoms plus demonstrably variable expiratory airflow support asthma; variability is a defining diagnostic feature. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Repeat objective testing when symptomatic or use an appropriate variability test: Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; diagnostic confirmation may require repeated or alternative testing. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Type 2 airway inflammation: Eosinophilic inflammation is a common asthma phenotype, involving pathways such as IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13; not all asthma is eosinophilic. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Bronchial hyperresponsiveness: Excessive airway narrowing to a stimulus is characteristic of hyperresponsive airways, although challenge results require clinical interpretation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
